profiles.meeting_scenario: A design review meeting at NorthBridge Bank to evaluate an existing proposal for an "Integrated Systemic Risk Monitor" that combines interbank exposures, market signals, and scenario analysis into a single internal dashboard for the Group Risk Committee. The context is a 12-week pilot that must be credible enough for senior management review and potentially adaptable for future regulatory discussions. The agenda is to review whether the current proposal is sufficiently integrated, what legal entities and exposure layers are covered, what data cadence the monitoring pack will use, which historical stress scenario will anchor the scenario library, and whether the design is ready to move into pilot build. The expected outcome is a conditional approval of the proposal with a short list of modifications, while both participants leave believing they have aligned on scope and readiness.

members.name: Elena Rossi
members.expertise: Systemic risk modelling, network analytics, model validation, stress testing
members.background: Elena is a former central-bank quantitative researcher who now leads model design for group-wide risk analytics at NorthBridge Bank, with particular focus on inter-entity contagion and cross-exposure modelling.
members.private_state: She wants the proposal approved without reopening the core methodology, because her team has already socialized the modelling approach with Model Risk and has limited capacity to rework the data architecture; she is mainly worried that a superficially polished pilot could later fail internal validation.
hidden_assumptions: When the proposal says the pilot will be 'board-ready,' that means the systemic risk indicator must already have documented assumptions, stable calibration logic, and a defensible validation note, even if the interface is still plain.

When people say 'group-wide coverage,' they naturally include material non-bank affiliates such as the broker-dealer, treasury vehicle, and funding conduit because contagion does not respect the regulated-bank perimeter.
A 'monthly monitoring pack' means month-end snapshots sourced from reconciled books-and-records positions, not daily feeds summarized into monthly charts.
The 'March stress case' refers to the March 2023 regional-bank liquidity episode because it is the most relevant recent benchmark for deposit flight and funding contagion.
An 'integrated' design implies cross-layer harmonization of exposures in the model logic, not merely co-locating separate indicators in one dashboard.

members.name: David Chen
members.expertise: Regulatory program delivery, executive reporting, risk data implementation, stakeholder management
members.background: David has spent a decade running enterprise regulatory-change programs across finance and risk functions, translating technical analytics into deliverables that can be demonstrated to executives, auditors, and supervisory visitors.
members.private_state: He wants a pilot that can be shown quickly to the Group Risk Committee as evidence of progress on firm-wide risk integration, and he is concerned that the design could become too academically heavy to deliver on the current quarter's timeline.
hidden_assumptions: When the proposal says the pilot will be 'board-ready,' that means the workflow, visuals, and commentary are polished enough for committee discussion, even if some model documentation remains in draft.

When people refer to 'group-wide coverage,' they mean the legal entities inside the current regulatory reporting perimeter, especially the top regulated banking subsidiaries already in existing governance packs.
A 'monthly monitoring pack' can be built from daily ingested data that is rolled up to monthly views, because executives expect trendlines rather than a single month-end point.
The 'March stress case' refers to the March 2020 COVID market-dislocation scenario already used in prior steering materials, making it easy to reuse narrative framing and committee expectations.
An 'integrated' design means one joined-up dashboard experience that presents multiple risk lenses consistently, even if the underlying indicators are still calculated separately.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as an integrated design
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both refer to the proposal as an 'integrated systemic risk monitor' and discuss whether the design is sufficiently integrated.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes 'integrated' means the exposure layers are harmonized in the analytical model so the overall indicator reflects interrelated effects across unsecured lending, derivatives, collateral, and payment flows.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes 'integrated' means the user sees one coherent dashboard that brings separate indicators together under one workflow and commentary structure, even if the calculations remain modular and only loosely linked.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both meanings are positive and professionally plausible in a design review, so each hears confirmation of their own interpretation when the other praises an 'integrated' approach.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both say the pilot should provide 'group-wide coverage' or 'full coverage for the pilot.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes this includes material non-bank affiliates and special funding entities that contribute to contagion pathways, even if they sit outside the standard regulatory reporting pack.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes this includes only the regulated entities already inside the bank's formal reporting perimeter, particularly the top banking subsidiaries reviewed by the Group Risk Committee.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Because both are speaking about coverage at a high level and both expect the other to know the organization's usual perimeter, neither thinks to enumerate legal entities during a meeting that is framed as a design review rather than a scoping workshop.

misalignment_points.topic: Which March stress episode anchors the scenario library
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both agree to 'use the March stress case' as the historical anchor for the scenario library.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is referring to the March 2023 regional-bank liquidity shock, seeing it as the appropriate benchmark for funding fragility, deposit concentration, and contagion through confidence channels.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is referring to the March 2020 COVID market-dislocation episode, because that is the established stress narrative from prior executive decks and can be reused with minimal change management.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both episodes are well-known, both are commonly shortened to 'the March event' internally, and each participant assumes the other is naturally referring to the most salient March stress in their own recent work context.

misalignment_points.topic: What makes the pilot board-ready and what monthly monitoring means
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that the design should be 'board-ready for the pilot' and support a 'monthly monitoring pack.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks board-ready means the indicator logic is defensible and documented, and that monthly monitoring means month-end reconciled snapshots suitable for model governance and repeatable committee use.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks board-ready means polished visuals and a usable committee narrative, and that monthly monitoring means trend reporting generated from daily data rolled into a monthly pack.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrases 'board-ready' and 'monthly monitoring' are standard executive shorthand, so the conversation can proceed smoothly without either side realizing they are using different acceptance standards and different implicit data cadence assumptions.
